name: Operational Excellence (OPS)
description: Operate, monitor, and continuously improve Couchbase cluster operations to deliver business value and mitigate risks.

questions.title: How do you notice a problem before users do?
questions.description: Watch resident ratio, latency, and failed cluster tasks, and page someone.

options.label: Watch resident ratio, Key-Value operations per second, and latency

risks.reason: If nobody watches resident ratio, the bucket can fall out of memory and start reading from disk before anyone notices.

improvements.title: Monitor the Data Service
improvements.description: Alert on resident ratio, Key-Value throughput, and latency for each service. A falling resident ratio means the working set no longer fits in memory.

options.label: Send cluster metrics to the same place as the rest of the platform

risks.reason: Metrics that stay inside the Couchbase UI are hard to compare with application latency during an incident.

improvements.title: Centralize cluster metrics
improvements.description: Scrape the Prometheus metrics endpoint, or use Capella's metrics integration, and send the data to the same system as the applications.

options.label: Turn on completed-request logging for slow SQL++ queries

risks.reason: A slow SQL++ query can use a large share of Query Service CPU and never appear in the application logs.

improvements.title: Record slow SQL++ queries
improvements.description: Use system:completed_requests, or the completed-request threshold, and review the slow statements.

options.label: Alert when a node is down, memory headroom is low, or a rebalance fails

risks.reason: Auto-failover and a failed rebalance need a person. A dashboard that nobody watches does not page anyone.

improvements.title: Page on cluster failures
improvements.description: Alert on node-down, low bucket memory headroom, failed rebalance, and a configuration change that does not finish.

questions.title: How do you add or remove nodes safely?
questions.description: A rebalance moves data. Do it in a quiet window and wait until it finishes.

options.label: Run rebalance in a planned window, not during peak traffic

risks.reason: A rebalance moves data across the network and disk. Doing that at peak adds load to the nodes that are still serving traffic.

improvements.title: Plan the rebalance window
improvements.description: Schedule node additions and removals outside the peak, and watch the rebalance until it finishes.

options.label: Use delta recovery when a node was offline briefly and still has its data files

risks.reason: A full recovery copies the whole data set again. Delta recovery copies only what changed, when the node's files are still valid.

improvements.title: Prefer delta recovery for a short outage
improvements.description: Choose delta recovery when the node still has its data. Use full recovery when the disk was replaced or the files are not trusted.

options.guidance: Delta recovery is not always possible. It needs the data files that were on the node before it failed.

options.label: Group node additions and removals instead of changing topology one node at a time all week

risks.reason: Each topology change starts a rebalance. A series of small changes keeps the cluster moving data for a long time.

improvements.title: Batch topology changes
improvements.description: Add or remove the nodes you already know you need in one change, then let that rebalance finish.

options.label: Watch rebalance, index build, and warmup until they finish

risks.reason: A rebalance or index build that looks idle in the UI can still be running. The next change should wait until it finishes.

improvements.title: Check the task list before the next change
improvements.description: On self-managed Server, use the tasks endpoint or the UI activity list. On Capella, use the activity view for the cluster.

questions.title: How do you automate Couchbase deployments and configuration management?
questions.description: Treat infrastructure as code to reduce manual toil and ensure consistency across database environments.

options.label: Define clusters, buckets, and roles in code

risks.reason: Settings changed only in the UI drift between environments and cannot be rebuilt the same way.

improvements.title: Keep cluster configuration in code
improvements.description: Use Terraform, Ansible, the Operator, or the Capella API so buckets, memory quotas, and roles are reviewed like application code.

options.label: Run Couchbase on Kubernetes with the Autonomous Operator

risks.reason: A Couchbase cluster on Kubernetes that is not managed by the Autonomous Operator is upgraded, failed over, and rebalanced by hand.

improvements.title: Use the Autonomous Operator
improvements.description: Let the Operator create the pods, run upgrades, and perform failover and rebalance. Do not operate the cluster with ad-hoc kubectl commands.

options.label: Keep index definitions in source control and deploy them in a pipeline, never from a framework at runtime

risks.reason: Manually applying index definitions in production bypasses peer review and can lock up query services if applied incorrectly.

improvements.title: Integrate database changes into pipelines
improvements.description: Store SQL++ index definitions next to the application and apply them in the pipeline. Do not let a framework create indexes on startup.

antiPatterns: Letting Spring Data or a similar framework create a primary index when the application starts

options.label: Keep memory quotas, bucket settings, and XDCR configuration in source control

risks.reason: Without version control, rolling back an erroneous cluster setting or identifying who made a change during an incident is nearly impossible.

improvements.title: Version control operational settings
improvements.description: Maintain a source-of-truth repository for all cluster tuning parameters, memory quotas, and cross-datacenter replication (XDCR) setups.

options.label: Run integration tests against a real Couchbase instance, not a mock

risks.reason: Mocks hide durability, timeout, and consistency behaviour that only appears against a real cluster.

improvements.title: Test against Couchbase in the pipeline
improvements.description: Run the critical paths in Docker, Testcontainers, or a Capella development cluster before release.

questions.title: How do you respond to operational events and database incidents?
questions.description: Establish standardized procedures to investigate and resolve issues quickly while minimizing human error.

options.label: Write the steps for failover, node replacement, and restore

risks.reason: During an incident, an unclear step is how a graceful failover becomes a hard failover, or a restore restores the wrong bucket.

improvements.title: Write the cluster runbooks
improvements.description: Document graceful failover, hard failover, node replacement, and restore, including who is allowed to run each one.

options.label: Write how to investigate slow queries, high indexer CPU, and XDCR lag

risks.reason: Without a shared sequence, two people troubleshoot the same incident in different orders and lose time.

improvements.title: Write the investigation steps
improvements.description: Start from the symptom: query timeouts, indexer CPU, disk queue, or replication lag, and list the first checks.

options.label: Review serious incidents and record what will change

risks.reason: If a serious incident is closed without a written cause and a change, the same failure is likely to happen again.

improvements.title: Review serious incidents
improvements.description: After a serious outage, write the timeline, the cause, and the change that should prevent a repeat.

questions.title: How do you upgrade while the cluster stays online?
questions.description: Swap in nodes on the new version. Check the SDK before you start.

options.label: Upgrade online with a swap rebalance, not a full restart

risks.reason: Restarting every node at once takes the cluster offline. Couchbase upgrades an online cluster by swapping nodes.

improvements.title: Swap in the new version
improvements.description: Add a node on the target version with the same services, remove one old node, and rebalance. Repeat. From 7.1 or 7.2 to 7.6.0 or 7.6.1, Index nodes must use this swap rebalance.

options.label: Check the SDK support matrix before the server upgrade

risks.reason: An SDK that is too old for the new server can fail to connect or can fail specific operations after the upgrade.

improvements.title: Match the SDK to the server version
improvements.description: Compare each application's SDK version with the compatibility matrix for the target server version before the upgrade starts.

options.label: Run the real queries and data shape in a test cluster before the upgrade

risks.reason: A server upgrade can change a query plan. A test that does not run the production queries will not show that.

improvements.title: Test the upgrade with production-like work
improvements.description: Restore a recent backup, or a masked copy, and run the important queries and writes against the target version.

options.label: Check indexes, balance, and application errors after the upgrade

risks.reason: An upgrade can finish in the UI while an index is still building or an application is returning new errors.

improvements.title: Check the cluster after the upgrade
improvements.description: Confirm rebalance is complete, indexes are online, and the application's error rate is back to normal.

options.label: Pin SDK versions and upgrade them on a cadence against the SDK support policy

risks.reason: Checking the compatibility matrix only at server upgrade time leaves applications on an SDK that is already out of support.

improvements.title: Track SDK versions like any other runtime
improvements.description: Record the SDK version in each service, compare it with the published support window, and schedule upgrades.

options.label: Scan the Couchbase SDK and its dependencies for known vulnerabilities

risks.reason: A supported server version does not mean the application SDK is free of published vulnerabilities.

improvements.title: Include the SDK in dependency scanning
improvements.description: Run the same vulnerability scan used for other libraries against the Couchbase SDK and the drivers it pulls in.

questions.title: How do you continually evaluate and improve your Couchbase operations?
questions.description: Establish continuous feedback loops to optimize processes, improve efficiency, and reduce operational toil over time.

options.label: Schedule regular audits of unused indexes and obsolete buckets

risks.reason: Accumulating legacy data structures and redundant indexes slowly degrades cluster efficiency and increases backup storage footprints.

improvements.title: Implement operational cleanup routines
improvements.description: Periodically review query catalogs and system metrics to identify and drop unused secondary indexes or deprecated development buckets.

options.label: Review upcoming queries and schema changes with the application team

risks.reason: Operating the database in a silo prevents operations teams from understanding upcoming application schema changes or shifting query access patterns.

improvements.title: Align operations with development roadmaps
improvements.description: Conduct regular technical reviews with developers to align index design, query optimization, and cluster capacity with upcoming application features.

options.label: Track and review key operational metrics (e.g., MTTR, failed queries) over time

risks.reason: Without tracking historical operational data, it is impossible to know if process changes are successfully reducing downtime or improving query latencies.

improvements.title: Perform operations metrics reviews
improvements.description: Hold recurring reviews of historical metrics to identify long-term trends, prioritize technical debt reduction, and validate previous improvements.

options.label: Review CPU, memory, and disk on a schedule and resize the cluster

risks.reason: Assuming a static capacity model prevents the organization from optimizing costs or scaling ahead of predictable traffic growth.

improvements.title: Iteratively assess cluster sizing
improvements.description: Routinely analyze CPU, memory, and IOPS consumption against baseline expectations to safely downscale over-provisioned nodes or scale up bottlenecks.

questions.title: How do you instrument applications that use Couchbase SDKs?
questions.description: See application latency separately from cluster latency, and connect a slow query back to the caller.

options.label: Send SDK traces and metrics to the same system as the application

risks.reason: Cluster dashboards do not show time spent in the SDK. A slow request then cannot be split into application time and database time.

improvements.title: Trace the SDK call
improvements.description: Enable the SDK tracer and meter and export them with the rest of the service. OpenTelemetry is the usual path.

options.label: Review SDK threshold logs and orphaned-response reports

risks.reason: The SDK already records slow and orphaned responses. They are useless if nobody reads them.

improvements.title: Put threshold logging on the operational checklist
improvements.description: Ship SDK threshold and orphan logs to the same place as application logs and review them after an incident.

options.label: Use ping or diagnostics in application readiness checks

risks.reason: A process that cannot reach the cluster still receives traffic when readiness only checks that the process is up.

improvements.title: Fail readiness when the cluster is unreachable
improvements.description: Call the SDK ping or diagnostics endpoint before the process is marked ready.

options.label: Set client_context_id on each SQL++ call so it can be found in completed requests

risks.reason: A slow query on the server cannot be tied to the application request unless both sides share an id.

improvements.title: Pass the request id into SQL++
improvements.description: Set client_context_id from the application request or trace id on each query.

questions.guidance: This question is for the team that owns the service, not the cluster administrators.
antiPatterns: Looking only at cluster dashboards when the latency is inside the client

questions.title: How is the Linux host set up for Couchbase?
questions.description: Couchbase wants RAM. The default Linux settings swap that RAM away and slow the node down.
questions.guidance: Capella manages the host. Answer this for self-managed Server, and for the machines under the Autonomous Operator.

options.label: Set vm.swappiness to 1 on current Linux, and to 0 only on kernels older than 3.5

risks.reason: Most Linux systems default to 60, so they swap Couchbase memory even when RAM is still free.

improvements.title: Set swappiness before the node joins the cluster
improvements.description: Set vm.swappiness to 1 and keep it in the image or the automation that builds nodes. Leave a modest amount of swap so the kernel can avoid killing the process, and do not treat swap as extra RAM.

options.label: Turn transparent huge pages off (enabled and defrag set to never)

risks.reason: Transparent huge pages can stall Couchbase and can lead to the process being killed.

improvements.title: Disable transparent huge pages on every Couchbase machine
improvements.description: Set both enabled and defrag to never, including after reboot. On Kubernetes, set this on the host. Containers do not use swap, so swappiness does not apply there.

name: Security (SEC)
description: Protect access controls, data structures, and key material across Couchbase deployments.

questions.title: How do you manage identities and permissions for people and machines accessing Couchbase?
questions.description: Centralize identity management and enforce the principle of least privilege across all database interactions.

options.label: Sign administrators in through the Capella organization identity provider

risks.reason: Local Capella users that are not tied to the company identity provider stay behind when people change roles.

improvements.title: Use organization single sign-on
improvements.description: Configure the Capella organization identity provider and remove shared local administrator accounts.

options.label: Sign administrators in through LDAP or SAML

risks.reason: Local cluster users are easy to leave enabled after a person leaves. LDAP or SAML ties access to the company directory.

improvements.title: Use LDAP or SAML for administrators
improvements.description: Configure LDAP or SAML for people. PAM is only for a local operating-system account and is not a directory. Application users stay as database users with their own roles.

options.label: Grant each user only the scopes and collections it needs

risks.reason: A user with cluster or bucket administration can read and change data it does not need.

improvements.title: Limit each user to its data
improvements.description: Create roles on the scopes and collections the user needs. Do not grant Application Access or Cluster Admin to an application.

options.label: Rotate database passwords on a schedule

risks.reason: A password that never changes stays valid after a person leaves or a config file is copied.

improvements.title: Rotate database credentials
improvements.description: Store the password in a secrets manager and rotate it. Update the application without putting the new password in source control.

questions.title: How do you detect and investigate security events in your Couchbase environment?
questions.description: Capture and analyze events from logs to gain visibility and take action on potential threats.

options.label: Turn on auditing for logins and administrative changes

risks.reason: Without an audit record, a changed password, role, or bucket setting cannot be traced to a person or time.

improvements.title: Enable audit logging
improvements.description: Enable Couchbase auditing for authentication and administrative events, and keep the events long enough for an investigation.

options.label: Send audit and server logs off the cluster

risks.reason: Logs that exist only on a node are lost if that node is replaced, and they are hard to search during an incident.

improvements.title: Forward logs off the node
improvements.description: Ship audit and server logs to the security or operations log system. Capella can export logs; self-managed clusters typically use a log shipper.

questions.title: How do you protect your Couchbase network resources?
questions.description: Apply multiple layers of defense to protect from external and internal network-based threats.

options.label: Allow database and admin traffic only from known networks

risks.reason: A Data Service port or the admin console that is open to the internet can be scanned and attacked.

improvements.title: Close the cluster to unknown networks
improvements.description: On Capella, use the allowed-IP list. On self-managed clusters, use security groups or firewall rules for the application networks and the admin network.

options.label: On Capella, connect from the private network instead of the public endpoint

risks.reason: The public Capella endpoint puts database traffic on the internet path. Private Link or VPC peering keeps it on the private network.

improvements.title: Use a private Capella connection
improvements.description: Use VPC peering or Private Link for application traffic. Keep the public endpoint closed unless a client truly has no private path.

questions.title: How do you protect Couchbase data in transit and at rest?
questions.description: Protect data integrity and confidentiality through end-to-end encryption mechanisms.

options.label: Require TLS for clients and for traffic between nodes

risks.reason: A client or replication connection without TLS can expose credentials and documents on the network.

improvements.title: Require TLS
improvements.description: Require TLS 1.2 or later for clients. On self-managed clusters, also enable node-to-node encryption. Capella encrypts client and inter-node traffic.

options.label: Encrypt data at rest

risks.reason: An unencrypted disk or backup volume can be read by anyone who copies the files.

improvements.title: Encrypt stored data
improvements.description: Capella encrypts data at rest. Use a customer-managed key when policy requires you to hold the key. On self-managed clusters, encrypt the disks or volumes.

options.label: Encrypt specific fields in the application when the database administrator must not be able to read them

risks.reason: Volume encryption does not hide a field from someone who can run a query. Field-level encryption does, for the fields you choose.

improvements.title: Encrypt the fields that must stay hidden
improvements.description: Use the SDK field-level encryption library for those fields. Queries cannot filter on an encrypted field unless you design for that.

options.guidance: Use this for fields such as national identifiers or secrets. It is not required for every document.

questions.title: How do you prepare for and respond to security incidents involving Couchbase?
questions.description: Preparation is critical to timely investigation and recovery from security incidents.

options.label: Encrypt backups and store them where the cluster cannot overwrite them

risks.reason: A backup that the same account can delete does not help after a mistake or ransomware. An unencrypted backup is a second copy of the data.

improvements.title: Protect the backup copies
improvements.description: Encrypt backup files. On self-managed clusters, cbbackupmgr can encrypt them. Keep the files in storage with its own credentials and a retention lock where the platform supports it.

options.label: Keep a tested emergency admin path for when the identity provider is down

risks.reason: If every administrator signs in through an identity provider, an identity-provider outage can lock everyone out of the cluster.

improvements.title: Test emergency admin access
improvements.description: Store a break-glass administrator in a vault, restrict who can use it, and test the sign-in on a schedule.

questions.title: How do applications authenticate and connect securely?
questions.description: Each service has its own identity, a secret that is not in source control, and a verified TLS connection.

options.label: Give each service its own least-privilege database user, never Administrator or a shared user

risks.reason: A shared or Administrator credential means every service can read and change every bucket.

improvements.title: Create one database user per service
improvements.description: Grant that user only the scopes and collections the service uses.

options.label: Load application credentials from a secrets manager at runtime

risks.reason: A password in a config file or in source control is copied into every environment and every log archive.

improvements.title: Fetch the database password at startup
improvements.description: Read the credential from the secrets manager when the process starts. Do not commit it.

options.label: Connect with couchbases:// and certificate verification left on

risks.reason: A trust-all or insecure TLS setting copied from a development laptop accepts any certificate in production.

improvements.title: Require verified TLS
improvements.description: Use the couchbases scheme and do not disable certificate verification outside a local sandbox.

options.label: Use a client certificate instead of a password where the platform supports mutual TLS

risks.reason: A password is a bearer secret. A client certificate ties the connection to a service identity.

improvements.title: Use mutual TLS where it is supported
improvements.description: Issue a certificate per service and turn off password authentication for that user when mutual TLS is available.

options.guidance: A unique user and a verified couchbases:// connection are the required controls. Mutual TLS is an additional option.

questions.guidance: Role-based access on the cluster is necessary, and it does not by itself describe how the application obtains its identity.

questions.title: How do you build secure application code on Couchbase?
questions.description: SQL++ is built with parameters, SDK logs do not contain document bodies, and review looks for Couchbase-specific mistakes.

options.label: Pass SQL++ values as named or positional parameters, never by concatenating user input

risks.reason: String concatenation in SQL++ is an injection flaw, and it also prevents the server from reusing a query plan.

improvements.title: Parameterize every SQL++ statement
improvements.description: Build the statement with placeholders and pass user input only in the parameter object.

options.label: Configure SDK log redaction so documents and personal data are not written to logs or traces

risks.reason: A debug log of a document body becomes a second, unmanaged copy of personal data.

improvements.title: Redact SDK and application logs
improvements.description: Turn on SDK redaction and keep document contents out of application traces.

options.label: In code review, reject a primary index, a collection-wide scan, and a query with no limit

risks.reason: A query that reads an entire collection returns more data than the feature needs and can overload the Query Service.

improvements.title: Add those checks to code review
improvements.description: Reject a change that adds a primary index, a scan of a whole collection, or a SQL++ statement with no LIMIT.

name: Reliability (REL)
description: Design for resilient node, availability zone, and regional failure recovery scenarios, ensuring workloads perform their intended functions correctly and consistently.

questions.title: How do you survive a lost node, rack, or zone?
questions.description: Replicas, separate failure domains, and enough nodes to fail one over.

options.label: Set a replica count that matches how many nodes you can lose

risks.reason: A bucket with no replicas is unavailable for the documents on a node as soon as that node is lost.

improvements.title: Set replicas on production buckets
improvements.description: Use at least one replica for production data. Use more only when the cluster has enough nodes to place them in different failure domains.

options.label: Place the active copy and its replicas in different racks or availability zones

risks.reason: If the active document and its replica sit in the same rack or zone, one failure removes both copies.

improvements.title: Separate copies across failure domains
improvements.description: On self-managed Server, define Server Groups and place one group in each zone or rack. Capella spreads nodes across zones when the cluster is deployed that way.

options.label: Run production on at least three nodes

risks.reason: Auto-failover stays off with one or two nodes, because the cluster cannot break a tie safely.

improvements.title: Use three or more nodes in production
improvements.description: Keep a one-node or two-node cluster for development only. Add an arbiter only when you still need a vote and cannot add a full data node.

options.label: Keep the same number of nodes in each server group

risks.reason: A smaller group holds more replica data, so it runs hotter and fails over less evenly.

improvements.title: Balance the server groups
improvements.description: Put the same number of Data nodes in each rack or zone. Capella places nodes for you when the cluster is deployed across zones.

options.label: If you have two server groups, add a third group with an arbiter so failover can reach a majority

risks.reason: Two equal groups can lose quorum when one group disappears. Auto-failover then does not run.

improvements.title: Add an arbiter in a third group
improvements.description: An arbiter runs only the Cluster Manager. Start from the smallest node you already use, watch CPU and RAM during rebalance, and keep it in its own rack, host, or zone.

options.guidance: Skip this when you already have three or more equal groups. The arbiter is the vote, not a place to store data.

options.label: Set auto-failover long enough to ignore a short network blip, and short enough to recover

risks.reason: A timeout that is too short fails a healthy node over during a blip. A timeout that is too long leaves clients waiting.

improvements.title: Set the auto-failover timeout
improvements.description: Choose the timeout with the application timeouts in mind, and record why that value was picked.

options.label: Choose durability levels that the replica and node count can actually satisfy

risks.reason: A durability level the topology cannot meet returns DurabilityImpossible as soon as one node is unavailable.

improvements.title: Match durability to the topology
improvements.description: Check each write's durability level against the bucket replica count and the number of nodes that must acknowledge it.

options.label: Keep documents at or under 20 MB and keys at or under 250 bytes

risks.reason: The server rejects a document larger than 20 MB and a key longer than 250 bytes. Finding that in production means the write path was not checked.

improvements.title: Enforce the document and key limits
improvements.description: Reject oversized documents and keys in the application. Plan how many collections you need before the data model is fixed.

questions.title: How do applications handle a short cluster outage?
questions.description: Let the SDK retry. Do not add a second retry loop.

options.label: Rely on the SDK default retry strategy and do not stack an application retry loop on top

risks.reason: An extra application retry loop on top of the SDK default causes retry storms. Retrying a write when the outcome is unknown can duplicate data.

improvements.title: Bound retries to the SDK and known outcomes
improvements.description: Keep the SDK retry strategy. Do not wrap it in another loop. Retry a non-idempotent mutation only after an unambiguous failure.

options.guidance: BestEffortRetryStrategy is already the default in SDK 3. Retry a non-idempotent write only when the failure is unambiguous.
antiPatterns: Adding a second retry loop around every SDK call
Retrying a write after an ambiguous timeout

options.label: Read from a replica when the active copy is unavailable and a slightly older document is acceptable

risks.reason: During failover, a read of the active copy waits until failover finishes. A replica read can return the last replicated document sooner.

improvements.title: Add a replica read for that path
improvements.description: Use getAnyReplica or getAllReplicas only for reads that can accept replica data. Do not use it for a read that must see the latest write.

options.guidance: Replica reads can return data that is one replication behind the active document.

options.label: Make writes safe to retry, or do not retry them when the result is unknown

risks.reason: Retrying a write whose result was lost can create a second document or apply the same business action twice.

improvements.title: Decide which writes are safe to retry
improvements.description: Use a stable document key. Retry a write only when the error says the write did not happen, or when repeating it does not change the outcome.

questions.title: How do you manage disaster recovery across different datacenters?
questions.description: A second site is a business decision. If the service must survive the loss of one datacenter, the copy in the other site has to be real, measured, and tested.

options.label: If a second site is required, replicate to it with XDCR and record the conflict mode

risks.reason: Backups restore to a point in time. They do not keep a second site current. If the business needs that, XDCR is the Couchbase mechanism, and its conflict mode is fixed at bucket creation.

improvements.title: Add a second site only when the target requires it
improvements.description: Configure XDCR to the recovery cluster and write down the conflict mode. If one site is enough, record that in the notes instead of adding a cluster.

options.label: Write the recovery point and recovery time, and check the design against them

risks.reason: Without a recovery point and a recovery time, nobody can tell whether backups or XDCR are enough.

improvements.title: Write the recovery targets
improvements.description: Record how much data you can lose and how long you can be down. Compare the backup interval and the replication lag with those numbers.

options.label: If a second site exists, practice the switch

risks.reason: A recovery design that has never been run often fails on DNS, connection strings, or application configuration.

improvements.title: Practice the site switch
improvements.description: On a schedule, point a test application at the recovery cluster and confirm the data and the access path.

options.guidance: Check this when a second site exists. A single-site design is recorded in the notes on the previous items.

questions.guidance: Leave these unchecked when a single site is an accepted decision, and write that decision in the notes. They are findings only when a second site is required and missing.

questions.title: How do you back up data and ensure its recoverability?
questions.description: Establish persistent data protection mechanisms and validate restoration workflows to recover from catastrophic loss.

options.label: Take scheduled backups and test a restore

risks.reason: A backup that has never been restored is an unverified copy. Accidental deletion and disk loss both need that copy.

improvements.title: Schedule backups and restore one
improvements.description: On Capella, use the Capella backup schedule. On self-managed clusters, use the Backup Service or cbbackupmgr. Restore into a non-production bucket and check the data.

options.label: Store Data, Index, and Analytics on persistent volumes

risks.reason: An emptyDir or other ephemeral disk is wiped when the pod is replaced, so the node has to rebuild from replicas or from backup.

improvements.title: Use persistent volumes
improvements.description: In the Autonomous Operator, set persistent volumes for the services that store data. Capella manages disks for you.

options.guidance: Capella manages storage for you. This control applies to clusters run by the Autonomous Operator.

questions.title: How do you manage cluster capacity to prevent resource-induced outages?
questions.description: Ensure the cluster has sufficient memory, CPU, and disk headroom to handle peak loads and automated failover events.

options.label: Keep enough free memory, CPU, and disk to lose one node

risks.reason: If the remaining nodes cannot hold the replica data and the traffic, failover of one node overloads the rest.

improvements.title: Size for one node down
improvements.description: Leave headroom so the surviving nodes can take the data and the traffic of one failed node.

questions.title: How do you test the resiliency of your Couchbase architecture?
questions.description: Stop a node while the application is running, and confirm clients recover.

options.label: On a schedule, stop a node and confirm the cluster recovers

risks.reason: A failover setting that has never been used can fail on server groups, disk, or networking the first time a node is really lost.

improvements.title: Practice a node failure
improvements.description: In a non-production cluster, stop one node and confirm failover, rebalance, and application errors behave as expected.

options.label: Test failover and rebalance under application load, including SDK timeouts and error handling

risks.reason: A cluster drill that no application is running does not show whether clients time out, retry, or duplicate writes.

improvements.title: Fail the cluster while the application is serving traffic
improvements.description: During a failover or rebalance test, watch client errors, ambiguous timeouts, and whether retries stay bounded.

questions.title: How do you manage the SDK connection lifecycle?
questions.description: One cluster connection lives for the life of the process and is shared by every request.

options.label: Create one long-lived Cluster object per process and share it across requests

risks.reason: Opening a Cluster connection per request exhausts connections and adds bootstrap latency to every call.

improvements.title: Share one Cluster connection
improvements.description: Create the Cluster object at startup and inject it. Do not construct it inside a request handler.

options.label: Call waitUntilReady at startup and fail if the cluster cannot be reached

risks.reason: A process that starts before it can reach Couchbase fails the first real user request instead of failing deployment.

improvements.title: Wait until the SDK is ready
improvements.description: Block startup on waitUntilReady and fail the deployment if it times out.

options.label: Bootstrap from DNS SRV or from more than one seed node

risks.reason: A single seed node is a single point of failure for every new process that needs to join the cluster.

improvements.title: Configure multiple bootstrap targets
improvements.description: Use a DNS SRV record or list several seed addresses in the connection string.

options.label: In a short-lived function, create the connection outside the handler and reuse it

risks.reason: A function that connects on every invocation spends the request on bootstrap and can exhaust cluster connections.

improvements.title: Reuse the connection across invocations
improvements.description: Initialize the Cluster object outside the handler so the next invocation reuses it. On Capella, a very short function can call the Data API instead of holding a SDK connection.

options.guidance: This applies to any Couchbase cluster behind a short-lived function. The Capella Data API is an extra option on Capella only.

options.label: Close the SDK connection when the application stops

risks.reason: A process that exits without closing leaves connections and sockets until the server times them out.

improvements.title: Disconnect on shutdown
improvements.description: Call disconnect or close from the process shutdown hook.

questions.guidance: This is the most common application-side production failure: a new connection for every request.
antiPatterns: new Cluster() inside a web request
A hardcoded single hostname as the only seed

questions.title: How do you set timeouts and handle SDK errors?
questions.description: Each operation has a timeout that fits the caller, and an unknown write result is not treated as a clean failure.

options.label: Set a timeout per operation type that fits the upstream API deadline

risks.reason: The SDK defaults, including a multi-second Key-Value timeout and a much longer query timeout, rarely match the business deadline.

improvements.title: Set explicit timeout budgets
improvements.description: Configure Key-Value, durable write, query, search, and transaction timeouts from the caller's latency budget.

options.label: Treat an ambiguous failure differently from a failure that is known not to have happened

risks.reason: Retrying after AmbiguousTimeout or DurabilityAmbiguous can apply a payment, an order, or a stock change twice.

improvements.title: Branch on ambiguous and unambiguous errors
improvements.description: On an ambiguous result, reconcile before retrying. Retry immediately only when the SDK reports that the operation did not happen.

options.label: If the application retries, use capped exponential backoff with jitter and do not stack it on SDK retries

risks.reason: Immediate retries from both the SDK and the application multiply load while the cluster is already unhealthy.

improvements.title: Cap and jitter any extra retry
improvements.description: Prefer the SDK retry strategy. An application retry needs a maximum delay, jitter, and a stop condition.

options.label: Bound how many asynchronous or reactive calls are in flight

risks.reason: Unbounded concurrency during recovery sends more work to a cluster that is already catching up.

improvements.title: Limit in-flight SDK calls
improvements.description: Set a concurrency limit on async and reactive pipelines and shed or queue work past that limit.

options.label: Degrade a read to a replica or to cached data when the primary read times out

risks.reason: A primary timeout becomes a user-facing error even when a replica or a cache could answer.

improvements.title: Define the fallback read
improvements.description: For read paths that allow it, fall back to a replica read or a cached value and tell the caller the data may be stale.

questions.guidance: An ambiguous timeout means the write may have succeeded. It is not the same error as a document that was not found.
antiPatterns: One timeout value for Key-Value and SQL++

name: Performance Efficiency (PERF)
description: Optimize SQL++ execution, access models, and cluster sizing for predictable low-latency responses. Sub-millisecond latency applies to Key-Value access, not to SQL++.

questions.title: How do you keep SQL++ fast?
questions.description: Use an index, avoid functions on indexed fields, and prepare statements that run often.

options.label: Cover frequent SQL++ queries with an index that contains the fields they return

risks.reason: A query that must fetch the document from the Data Service after the index lookup moves much more data and takes longer.

improvements.title: Cover the frequent queries
improvements.description: Put the filter fields and the returned fields in the index when the query runs often. Confirm with EXPLAIN that the plan does not fetch the document.

options.label: Do not wrap an indexed field in a function inside WHERE

risks.reason: LOWER(name) = 'a' or a similar function on an indexed field stops the planner from using a bounded index scan. The query can fall back to a wider scan. That is not always a primary-index scan.

improvements.title: Keep predicates usable by the index
improvements.description: Store the value in the form you search for, such as a lowercase field, instead of wrapping the indexed field in LOWER() or another function.

options.label: Use Search for text search instead of many extra secondary indexes

risks.reason: A secondary index is a poor fit for ad-hoc text search across many fields. Search is built for that access pattern.

improvements.title: Use Search for text queries
improvements.description: Create a Search index for the text fields. Flex Indexes let SQL++ use that Search index when the query qualifies.

options.guidance: Skip this when the workload has no text search.

options.label: Use prepared statements for SQL++ that runs often with different values

risks.reason: Sending a new statement text for the same query shape makes the Query Service parse and plan it again.

improvements.title: Prepare statements that run often
improvements.description: Use SDK parameters so the statement text stays stable. The server can then reuse the plan. This is the performance side of the injection control in Security.

questions.title: How are client data access paths and document models structured?
questions.description: Align storage models and data access strategies with the native strengths of the Couchbase Key-Value architecture.

options.label: Read and write one known document with a Key-Value call, not with SQL++

risks.reason: SQL++ for a document you already know by id adds a query plan and an index lookup. The Key-Value get or upsert goes to the Data Service directly.

improvements.title: Use Key-Value for a known id
improvements.description: Use get, insert, replace, or upsert when the document id is known. Use SQL++ when you must find documents by a field.

options.label: Shape documents around one access, and update a single field with a Sub-Document call

risks.reason: A document that grows without a limit, or an update that rewrites the whole document to change one field, moves too much data.

improvements.title: Match the document to the access
improvements.description: Keep one document for one access path. Use a Sub-Document mutation when you change a field and do not need to send the rest.

options.label: Use Eventing instead of polling when the cluster should react to a change

risks.reason: A client that polls for changes adds a steady query load. Eventing runs when the document changes.

improvements.title: React on the server when polling is the current design
improvements.description: Move that reaction into an Eventing function if it belongs next to the data. A message bus is still a valid design when the consumer is outside the cluster.

options.guidance: Polling is the problem. Eventing is one Couchbase option, not the only one.

options.label: Design document keys for direct lookup and avoid a single hot key

risks.reason: A key that every request updates, or a model that can only be read by a query, bypasses the Key-Value service.

improvements.title: Make the common read a key lookup
improvements.description: Put the access key in the document ID. Split a hot counter or lock document when one key receives a disproportionate share of writes.

options.label: Review framework-generated SQL++ with EXPLAIN and keep primary indexes out of production

risks.reason: Frameworks such as Spring Data can create a primary index or emit a query that scans the whole collection.

improvements.title: Treat generated SQL++ as production code
improvements.description: Capture the SQL++ the framework sends, run EXPLAIN, and fail the build if the plan uses a primary index.

options.label: Fetch only the fields the caller needs, with a SQL++ projection or a Sub-Document lookup

risks.reason: Reading the whole document to use one field increases network cost and client memory.

improvements.title: Project or use lookupIn
improvements.description: Return the required fields from SQL++, or use the SDK Sub-Document API when the key is already known.

options.label: Update counters with an atomic increment or decrement

risks.reason: A read-modify-write counter loses updates and creates contention on one document.

improvements.title: Use the atomic counter API
improvements.description: Replace read-modify-write counter updates with the SDK increment and decrement operations.

questions.title: How do you size each Couchbase service?
questions.description: Data, Query, Index, and Search do not want the same hardware.

options.label: Run heavy Query, Index, or Search work on its own nodes when they contend with Data

risks.reason: Query, Index, and Search can steal CPU and RAM from the Data service and slow key-value reads.

improvements.title: Separate services that contend
improvements.description: Put Data on its own nodes when Query or Index load moves key-value latency. A small cluster can still share services if you have measured that it is fine.

options.label: Give the Index service enough RAM that indexes stay in memory

risks.reason: An index that does not fit in its RAM quota reads from disk and slows every query that uses it.

improvements.title: Size the Index service
improvements.description: Watch the index resident ratio. New indexes use the Plasma storage engine. Add Index nodes or RAM before that ratio falls and queries start hitting disk.

options.label: Pick Magma or Couchstore for the size of the bucket

risks.reason: Couchstore is a good fit when the dataset stays in memory. Magma is the better fit when the bucket is larger than memory.

improvements.title: Match the storage engine to the bucket
improvements.description: Use Magma for a large bucket. Keep Couchstore when the working set fits in RAM. The engine is chosen per bucket and is awkward to change later.

options.guidance: Capella uses Magma by default. On Server 8.0 and later, Magma is the recommended engine for most buckets. Couchstore fits a small dataset that stays in memory. Reading a document from disk is still a disk read.

questions.title: How do you maintain optimal query execution plans and database statistics?
questions.description: The query planner needs fresh statistics. The Index Advisor is a helper, not a required control.

options.label: Run UPDATE STATISTICS on collections whose data shape changes

risks.reason: Without statistics, the cost-based optimizer has little information about how many documents match a predicate and can choose a poor index.

improvements.title: Refresh collection statistics
improvements.description: Run UPDATE STATISTICS on the collections used by complex queries after large loads or big data changes.

options.label: Use the Index Advisor (ADVISE) when a slow query has no obvious index

risks.reason: ADVISE suggests an index for a statement. It does not replace EXPLAIN, and it is not required for every query.

improvements.title: Ask ADVISE for a starting index
improvements.description: Run ADVISE on the slow statement, then check the suggestion with EXPLAIN and with the indexes you already have.

options.guidance: A missing visit to the Index Advisor is not itself a defect.

questions.title: How do your client applications efficiently interact with the database cluster?
questions.description: Move many documents in batches, page through large results, and test with realistic data.

options.label: When loading many documents, use the SDK bulk or reactive API with a bounded batch

risks.reason: One HTTP-style call per document, waiting for each response, turns a load into a long sequence of round trips.

improvements.title: Batch large loads
improvements.description: Use the SDK bulk helpers or a bounded set of concurrent operations. Set the batch size from a test, not from an unlimited loop.

options.guidance: Check this if the application imports or updates many documents. A request that touches one document does not need it.

options.label: Defer index builds while a large import is running

risks.reason: Building every index while millions of documents are loading makes the import and the index build slower together.

improvements.title: Build indexes after the import
improvements.description: Create the indexes with defer_build, load the data, then run BUILD INDEX.

options.guidance: This applies to a bulk load, not to everyday writes.

options.label: Stream large results and paginate with a keyset instead of a large OFFSET

risks.reason: A large OFFSET still reads and discards every skipped row on each page.

improvements.title: Page with a keyset
improvements.description: Stream SDK results and continue from the last key or document ID instead of increasing OFFSET.

options.label: Set and test batch size and parallelism instead of leaving them unbounded

risks.reason: An unbounded fan-out saturates the cluster during recovery and during a bulk job.

improvements.title: Cap in-flight work
improvements.description: Choose a batch size and a concurrency limit, then measure them against a realistic data set.

options.label: Performance-test with realistic document sizes and key distribution

risks.reason: A test of tiny uniform documents hides the working set and the hot keys production will have.

improvements.title: Load-test the real shape of the data
improvements.description: Use a tool such as cbc-pillowfight or YCSB with production-like sizes, TTLs, and key distribution.

options.label: Use a Key-Value range scan for key-ordered batch work instead of adding an index only for that job

risks.reason: An index created only so a batch job can walk keys adds memory and write cost to the cluster.

improvements.title: Prefer a KV range scan for key ranges on Server 7.6+
improvements.description: When the job only needs documents in key order, use the SDK range scan instead of a secondary index.

questions.title: How do you optimize Full Text Search (FTS) and Analytics workloads?
questions.description: Answer this only if the workload uses Search or Analytics. A cluster with neither service should leave these unchecked.

options.label: Run large analytical scans on Analytics, not on the operational Query Service

risks.reason: A full-collection aggregation on the Query Service uses the same CPU as the application's SQL++.

improvements.title: Move heavy scans to Analytics
improvements.description: Use the Analytics service for long scans and ad-hoc aggregates. Leave the Query Service for the application's operational queries.

options.guidance: Skip this when the workload has no analytical scans.

options.label: Partition a Search index that is too large for one node

risks.reason: One large Search index can use more memory and disk than a single Search node can hold.

improvements.title: Partition the large Search index
improvements.description: Set index partitions so the Search index is spread across Search nodes.

options.guidance: Only for a Search index that has outgrown one node.

options.label: Index only the Search fields you query, with an explicit type mapping

risks.reason: The default dynamic mapping indexes every field. The Search index then grows with data the application never searches.

improvements.title: Turn off dynamic mapping
improvements.description: Define the document type and the child fields that Search should index.

options.guidance: Only if you use Search.

questions.guidance: Search and Analytics are separate services. They are not required for a Key-Value or SQL++ application.

name: Cost Optimization (COST)
description: Run Couchbase systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point by right-sizing infrastructure, managing data lifecycles, and tracking resource attribution.

questions.title: How do you govern and monitor your Couchbase resource usage and costs?
questions.description: Establish policies and procedures to monitor, appropriately allocate, and alert on costs associated with your database workloads.

options.label: Identify cost attribution using comprehensive resource tagging

risks.reason: Without tagging underlying instances or Kubernetes pods, organizations cannot track resources over their lifetime, making it impossible to attribute database costs to specific business units or applications.

improvements.title: Implement a tagging scheme
improvements.description: Gather stakeholders to define a tagging schema for all underlying Couchbase infrastructure to enable cost allocation and chargebacks.

options.label: Alert when cluster cost or size moves outside the expected range

risks.reason: A cluster that scales up, or a network bill that jumps, can run for days before anyone notices.

improvements.title: Alert on cost and size
improvements.description: On Capella, use the cost and sizing views. On a self-managed cluster in a cloud account, alert on the account spend and on unexpected node growth.

options.label: Review N+1 queries, polling, and unbounded scans before adding Query or Index nodes

risks.reason: The usual reason a cluster is oversized is the application access pattern, not a shortage of nodes.

improvements.title: Fix the access pattern before buying capacity
improvements.description: Identify polling loops, per-row queries, and collection-wide scans, and remove them before scaling the Query or Index service.

options.label: Make per-service usage visible with collections, users, and rate limits or quotas

risks.reason: A shared cluster with one database user cannot show which service is driving cost.

improvements.title: Separate tenants inside the cluster
improvements.description: Give each service its own user and collection, and apply quotas or rate limits where the server version supports them.

questions.title: How do you optimize Couchbase compute and infrastructure costs?
questions.description: Select the appropriate resource type, size, and pricing models to meet workload performance needs at the lowest cost.

options.label: For a steady cloud footprint, use the provider's committed pricing

risks.reason: A database that runs all month on on-demand cloud prices pays the highest rate for a predictable load.

improvements.title: Price the steady footprint
improvements.description: Review committed pricing for the nodes you always run. This does not apply to hardware you already own.

options.guidance: On-premises hardware does not have a reserved-instance price. Leave this unchecked and note that.

options.label: Scale Capella compute from observed demand rather than a fixed oversized cluster

risks.reason: A fixed Capella cluster sized for a peak that never arrives is paid for all month.

improvements.title: Scale Capella from measured demand
improvements.description: Review Capella sizing against CPU, memory, and query load, and change the cluster size when the trend is sustained.

options.label: Scale Autonomous Operator clusters with Kubernetes autoscaling tied to real service metrics

risks.reason: The Operator can add nodes, but a CPU target that ignores index or query memory still stalls the cluster or overpays for nodes.

improvements.title: Autoscale the Operator from service metrics
improvements.description: Use the Autonomous Operator with Kubernetes autoscaling based on the service that is actually saturated, not a single cluster-wide CPU target.

options.label: Plan self-managed capacity changes; Server has no built-in cluster autoscaler

risks.reason: Waiting for a node to run out of memory, then adding hardware by hand, is the failure mode self-managed clusters actually hit.

improvements.title: Keep a capacity plan for self-managed Server
improvements.description: Track headroom and schedule node additions. Do not document a native Server autoscaler that the product does not provide.

questions.title: How do you optimize Couchbase data storage costs?
questions.description: Manage data lifecycles, limit index overhead, and align storage models to reduce unnecessary block storage expenses.

options.label: Use an ephemeral bucket only for data that can be dropped on restart

risks.reason: A cache that is stored in a Couchbase bucket still writes to disk unless the bucket is ephemeral.

improvements.title: Use an ephemeral bucket for a real cache
improvements.description: Choose ephemeral when losing the data on restart is acceptable. Do not use it for data you must keep.

options.guidance: Most application data should stay in a Couchbase bucket that persists.

options.label: Identify and remove redundant or duplicate indexes

risks.reason: Unused or redundant indexes waste expensive memory quota and disk space while simultaneously slowing down mutation write performance.

improvements.title: Establish index cleanup routines
improvements.description: Regularly audit index usage statistics via system catalogs, removing indexes that do not support active query workflows.

questions.title: How do you manage data transfer and network costs?
questions.description: Plan and monitor data transfer charges to make architectural decisions that minimize operational networking expenses.

options.label: Keep Capella traffic on a private connection so it is not billed as public egress

risks.reason: Traffic from an application to the public Capella endpoint can be charged as internet egress.

improvements.title: Avoid public egress to Capella
improvements.description: Use Private Link or VPC peering for the application path. This is the cost side of the private-network control in Security.

options.guidance: The security control is the one that must be checked. This item is the cost reason for the same design.

options.label: If you use XDCR across regions, replicate only the data the other region needs

risks.reason: Cross-region replication is billed as data transfer. Copying a whole bucket copies data the other site may never read.

improvements.title: Filter cross-region replication
improvements.description: Filter XDCR by collection or filter expression so only the required documents cross the region boundary.

options.guidance: Leave this unchecked when there is no cross-region XDCR.

options.label: On Server 7.6.2 or later, prefer a replica in the same zone when a local copy is acceptable

risks.reason: In cloud pricing, a read that crosses an availability zone can be billed even when a copy exists in the local zone.

improvements.title: Prefer the local zone for replica reads
improvements.description: Configure the SDK preferred server group where the server version supports it. Do not use this to bypass a read that must see the latest write.

options.guidance: On-premises networks may not bill cross-zone traffic. Leave this unchecked when it does not apply.

options.label: Leave SDK compression on and trim payloads with projections or Sub-Document operations

risks.reason: Shipping a full document when the caller needs one field increases data-transfer cost.

improvements.title: Send fewer bytes per call
improvements.description: Keep SDK compression enabled and fetch only the fields the request uses.

questions.title: How do you manage the lifecycle of your Couchbase environments to prevent waste?
questions.description: Implement resource management from inception to end-of-life, shutting down unused resources to reduce waste.

options.label: Turn off or schedule a pause for non-production Capella clusters outside business hours

risks.reason: A development or test Capella cluster that runs all night and all weekend is billed while nobody is using it.

improvements.title: Stop non-production Capella clusters
improvements.description: Turn the cluster off, or schedule that, outside working hours. Production clusters should not be paused this way.

options.guidance: Capella exposes cluster on/off and scheduling. Self-managed Server does not have a hibernation feature.

options.label: Audit and remove sample buckets, unused data, and orphaned volumes

risks.reason: Retaining unused sample data buckets or detached physical disk volumes incurs ongoing block storage fees for zero business value.

improvements.title: Automate unused asset cleanup
improvements.description: Ensure development Sample Buckets are not deployed in higher environments, and actively monitor and delete orphaned block storage volumes.

name: Data Management & Consistency (DATA)
description: Manage consistency controls, write durability guarantees, and logical organization shapes across evolving Couchbase datasets.

questions.title: How do you manage write durability and concurrency controls?
questions.description: Balance application data integrity guarantees with network latency, and ensure safe concurrent document modifications.

options.label: Set a durability level on writes that must survive a node loss

risks.reason: A write that returns before it is replicated can be lost if the active node fails first.

improvements.title: Set durability on the writes that need it
improvements.description: Use Majority, or a stronger level the topology can meet, for those writes. A cache write can stay at the default.

options.label: Use the document CAS when two callers can update the same document

risks.reason: A read-modify-write that ignores CAS overwrites the other caller's change.

improvements.title: Use CAS for concurrent updates
improvements.description: Read the document, change it, and replace it with the CAS you read. Retry when the CAS no longer matches.

options.label: Use getAndLock only for a proven hot document, and keep the lock short

risks.reason: getAndLock as the normal update path holds a lock on the document and lowers throughput. CAS is the usual control.

improvements.title: Keep pessimistic locks rare
improvements.description: Do not lock every document. If a measurement shows one hot key, use getAndLock with a short lock time and do not hold that lock across another network call.

options.guidance: Pessimistic locking is the exception. A missing getAndLock is not itself a risk.
antiPatterns: Holding a pessimistic lock across a network call

questions.title: How do you structure data lifecycles and logical isolation?
questions.description: Control database volume growth and manage document schema transformations over time using multi-tenant boundaries.

options.label: Organize datasets logically using Scopes and Collections

risks.reason: Dumping unrelated datasets into a single bucket complicates index design, safety boundaries, and data lifecycles, while creating separate buckets adds heavy cluster overhead.

improvements.title: Adopt a clean Scopes and Collections taxonomy
improvements.description: Group data structures logically into Scopes and Collections within a bucket to simplify access controls, indexing, and multi-tenant isolation.

options.label: Set a TTL on documents that should disappear, such as sessions and one-time tokens

risks.reason: A cleanup job that deletes old documents can fall behind. A TTL lets the Data Service expire them.

improvements.title: Expire temporary documents with a TTL
improvements.description: Set the TTL on the document or on the collection. Do not set a TTL on data that must be kept.

options.guidance: Leave this unchecked when the bucket has no temporary documents.

options.label: On replace or upsert, keep the existing TTL when the document must still expire

risks.reason: A replace that does not preserve expiry sets the TTL to 0. The document then never expires.

improvements.title: Preserve expiry on later writes
improvements.description: Set the SDK preserve-expiry option on replace and upsert for documents whose lifetime is a TTL.

options.guidance: This matters only for documents that use a TTL.

options.label: Store a schema version on the document and decide how old documents are updated

risks.reason: Old and new document shapes in the same collection cannot be told apart without a version field. Readers then fail or ignore fields.

improvements.title: Version the document shape
improvements.description: Add a version field. Either upgrade the document when it is read, or run a backfill. Record which one you chose.

questions.title: How do you balance SQL++ query consistency with performance?
questions.description: Tune index scan consistency to meet business requirements without unnecessarily degrading query throughput.

options.label: Choose scan consistency per query instead of one setting for the whole application

risks.reason: request_plus makes the query wait until the index has caught up, which is slower. not_bounded can miss a write the same session just made. One global setting is wrong for both cases.

improvements.title: Set consistency on the query that needs it
improvements.description: Use not_bounded for reads that can be slightly behind. Use request_plus or a mutation token only when that query must see specific writes.

options.label: When a session must see its own write, pass the mutation token (at_plus) instead of using request_plus everywhere

risks.reason: request_plus waits for the index to catch up with every mutation, not only the one from this session.

improvements.title: Use at_plus for read-your-own-writes
improvements.description: Pass the mutation token from the write into the query with at_plus or consistentWith.

questions.title: How do you maintain atomicity across multiple document modifications?
questions.description: One document is updated atomically by a single Key-Value write. Use a transaction only when one action must change several documents together.

options.label: Use Couchbase transactions when one action must commit several documents together

risks.reason: Separate writes can leave the first document updated and the second unchanged if the process stops.

improvements.title: Use a transaction for that action
improvements.description: Use the SDK transaction API or a SQL++ transaction. Do not invent a two-phase commit in application code.

options.guidance: Leave this unchecked when each action updates one document.

options.label: Update one field with a Sub-Document call when you do not need to send the whole document

risks.reason: Rewriting a large document to change one field moves the whole document and raises the chance of a CAS mismatch.

improvements.title: Use a Sub-Document update for one field
improvements.description: Use mutateIn for a field change. A small document can still be replaced in full.

options.label: Keep a transaction short, on a limited number of documents, and free of calls to other systems

risks.reason: A transaction that calls another service, or touches too many documents, holds resources until it expires.

improvements.title: Shorten the transaction
improvements.description: Do the Couchbase writes inside the transaction. Call other systems before or after it.

options.guidance: Only if the application uses Couchbase transactions.

options.label: Treat an ambiguous commit as unknown until you know whether it committed

risks.reason: A lost response after commit does not mean the transaction failed. Starting it again can apply the business action twice.

improvements.title: Handle an ambiguous commit
improvements.description: Do not retry the business action until the transaction outcome is known. Decide where the transaction cleanup metadata collection lives.

options.guidance: Only if the application uses Couchbase transactions.

questions.guidance: If every business action changes one document, say so in the notes and leave the transaction items unchecked.

questions.title: How do you handle XDCR conflicts when both sites accept writes?
questions.description: Answer this only for active-active replication. A single cluster has no conflict mode to choose.

options.label: Choose the XDCR conflict mode when the bucket is created, and use the same mode on every bucket in the replication

risks.reason: The mode is fixed at bucket creation. Timestamp mode with drifting clocks can keep the wrong document. Buckets in one replication must use the same mode.

improvements.title: Record the conflict mode before the bucket exists
improvements.description: Write down sequence-number or timestamp before the bucket exists. Use timestamp when clocks stay in sync. Use the same choice on every bucket in that replication.

options.guidance: You cannot change the mode later. Sequence number is the default. Timestamp mode is easier to reason about when NTP is on and clock drift is watched.
antiPatterns: Timestamp mode without NTP, or without watching clock drift
Replicating buckets that use different conflict modes

options.label: Filter XDCR so a remote cluster receives only the collections it needs

risks.reason: Replicating every collection sends data the other site may not be allowed to store, and it uses bandwidth.

improvements.title: Filter the replication
improvements.description: Use a collection mapping or a filter expression. Do not replicate a collection only because it sits in the same bucket.

options.guidance: Only for an active-active or active-passive XDCR setup.

options.label: Turn on XDCR conflict logging when both clusters accept writes

risks.reason: Without a conflict log, you cannot see which document version was kept after a conflict.

improvements.title: Log XDCR conflicts
improvements.description: Enable conflict logging and review it when the application reports a lost update.

options.guidance: Only when both sides of the replication accept writes.

questions.guidance: Conflict resolution is chosen when the bucket is created and cannot be switched later.

questions.title: How do you automate complex data enrichment and reactive workflows?
questions.description: Use Eventing when a change in the cluster should run server-side logic. Do not build a private DCP client for a new workload.

options.label: Use an Eventing function for a reaction that should run inside the cluster

risks.reason: Polling from an application adds a steady read load. Eventing runs when a document changes.

improvements.title: Use Eventing for that reaction
improvements.description: Keep the function small. Give it a role that can touch only the collections it needs.

options.guidance: A worker outside the cluster, fed by the Kafka connector, is a valid alternative.

options.label: Use an Eventing timer for work that must run later, if you already use Eventing

risks.reason: A separate scheduler is extra machinery when an Eventing function already owns that workflow.

improvements.title: Use an Eventing timer
improvements.description: Create the timer from the function that owns the document. Do not add Eventing only to get a timer.

options.guidance: Only if you already run Eventing.

options.label: Give each Eventing function a role limited to the collections it uses

risks.reason: A function that runs as a broad administrator can change collections outside its job.

improvements.title: Limit the function's role
improvements.description: Create a user for the function and grant only the collections it reads and writes.

options.guidance: Only if you run Eventing.

options.label: Take a change feed from Eventing or a supported connector, not from a custom DCP client

risks.reason: A private DCP client has to handle flow control, failover, and rollback. Those are already handled by Eventing and the supported connectors.

improvements.title: Use a supported change feed
improvements.description: Prefer Eventing or the Kafka connector. Do not write a new DCP consumer.

options.label: Use the same date, number, and enum formats in every SDK language that reads the documents

risks.reason: One service writing a string date and another writing an epoch makes queries and comparisons disagree.

improvements.title: Publish the field formats
improvements.description: Agree the representation of dates, numbers, and enums and check it in review when a second language is added.

questions.guidance: Eventing is optional. The change-feed and data-format items apply to every application.
